records.finding: Proposes an event-scoped requires link from Egyptian papyrus writing support to the physical recording of Merer’s hieratic logbooks. The surviving sheets carry the actual script. The Abydos U-j bone and ivory tags supply a separately dated archaeological witness to the early sign system. The relationship of Egyptian writing to Uruk proto-cuneiform and the significance of separate painted marks on vessels remain open. Also proposes a distinct local receiver at Serabit el-Khadim. Several alphabetic signs there preserve recognizable Egyptian sign forms given Semitic consonantal values; an adapts link describes the graphic inheritance. The Temple of Hathor sphinx gives a local witness of the two scripts used on one object. The early Egyptian source record describes the sign repertoire, and a handoff from any individual Abydos object or a route from Serabit to Lachish remains unresolved.

records.finding: The existing conditional layer 4c evidence is retained. Localized polish corroborates ornament use, while reported chipped holes have several possible causes. The separate Taforalt assemblage shares some shell selections and wear patterns and shows later regional bead use. A specific exchange route, descent from Bizmoune, and a link to the separate South African Blombos beadmaking remain unresolved.

sources.note: Most holes are partly natural. The authors identify chipping, polish and localized wear and discuss how the assemblage fits wider regional evidence. Table 1 shows conflicting dating signals.

sources.note: Original report of separate Moroccan assemblage at Taforalt. The authors consider possible exchange and long-distance networks from transport of shells; some investigators overlap with Bizmoune.

records.next: Seek a securely dated intervening assemblage and comparable shell collection, modification and wear sequences tied to a demonstrable transport or contact route.

records.finding: The reported M1 beadwork and probable stringing are retained. Separate experiments on shell wear refine how some shells may have been arranged. Ochre residues and experimental reproduction with coated thread leave multiple possible pathways for the pigment and provide no tie to the earlier M3 mixture.

sources.locator: Vanhaeren et al. 2013, abstract, figs. 1 and 10–11, Discussion
sources.note: A cluster of 24 perforated shells probably came from one beadwork. The study adds direct observations and comparison experiments while sharing authors and specimens with the original reports; stringing patterns are inferred.

sources.locator: Henshilwood et al. 2011, pp. 219–221, figs. 2–4 and manufacturing interpretation
sources.note: Residues and associated tools support production and storage of two M3 mixtures. The authors infer powder preparation on stone surfaces and mixing in shells. Final use is unknown.

records.next: Compare in situ residues on specific shells and sediments with contemporaneous preparation evidence. Seek preserved stringing material if possible and distinguish transfer during wear from deliberate application.

records.finding: The two M3 preparation and storage kits are retained. Pinnacle Point documents earlier powder preparation in a different context. The later Blombos cross-hatched marks were attributed to an ochre crayon on silcrete. Neither comparison identifies a predecessor or a final use for the particular M3 mixture.

sources.locator: Henshilwood et al. 2018, abstract and figs. 2–3
sources.note: Different specimen from much later Blombos strata. Comparative microscopy and experiments distinguish a crayon from liquid paint. Researchers overlap with the mixture study.

records.next: Look for residues of the prepared mixture directly on a dated implement or treated object from an associated deposit. Test the correspondence in composition, use-wear and stratigraphy.

records.finding: Established affinity only. Independent excavation and laboratory observations support one shared principle with earlier copper beads at Çayönü, hammering metal to sheet and rolling it into a tube. Historical prerequisites, transmission, and descent to later iron smelting remain deferred. Johnson and colleagues corroborate meteoritic origin and the sheet seam on a distinct Gerzeh specimen. The studies’ thermal inferences differ and apply to different samples.

sources.note: Identifies the two burial contexts and separately pictures a modern re-stringing of stone and faience beads. Neutron images of three Petrie Museum iron beads show rolled seams. Intermittent annealing is inferred.

records.next: Seek pre-Gerzeh Egyptian metal sheets or tubes with directly comparable manufacturing traces and chronological context. A transferred technique requires a documented path; later ore smelting also requires separate evidence.

records.finding: The figurative-scene event and minimum age are retained. The sampled overlying calcite constrains the date but gives no pigment recipe. Hematite identifications at Sumpang Bita 2 apply to two motifs at another cave. The older Liang Metanduno date belongs to a hand stencil and is a minimum age for a different artifact. A shared tradition or specific technique transfer into the Leang Karampuang scene remains unresolved.

records.next: Find published composition or tool traces from this panel and securely matched nearby contexts. Compare technique and chronology before considering continuity.

records.finding: Early glazed steatite and synthetic quartz-body faience differ in their substrate. Badarian beads demonstrate a glazed-stone practice in Egypt and some analyzed steatite samples suggest cementation. The faience microscopy series of Tite and colleagues starts at the Middle Kingdom. Neither source independently connects Badarian glazing to the earliest Egyptian or Near Eastern faience production. The modern re-strung Gerzeh assemblage does not establish technological dependence between faience and iron beads.
